title: Context and Brakes: How Cells Read TGF-β

scenes.visual: Dark navy canvas carrying the exact colour map from the first film. Inside the glowing golden nuclear rim (labelled 'Schematic' in a small corner tag), the emerald and violet Smad trimer drifts above a gently waving DNA strand. Crisp white title fades in and out across the upper band: 'Context and Brakes: How Cells Read TGF-β'.

scenes.tts: In the first film, TGF beta bridged two kinases and sent a Smad complex into the nucleus. Yet that same complex halts many healthy epithelial cells and can help late tumours spread. How can one signal give opposite answers, and what holds it back?
scenes.caption: In the first film, TGF-β bridged two kinases and sent a Smad complex into the nucleus. Yet that same complex halts many healthy epithelial cells and can help late tumours spread. How can one signal give opposite answers, and what holds it back?
scenes.visual: Carried nuclear view from s00. The emerald/violet Smad trimer carrying yellow phosphates glides across the nuclear rim. Below it, two contrasting outcome icons pulse softly on either side of the DNA strand: a soft teal 'Stop dividing' bar on the left and a migrating cell outline labelled 'Late tumour: move' on the right.
scenes.narration: In the first film, TGF-β bridged two kinases and sent a Smad complex into the nucleus. Yet that same complex halts many healthy epithelial cells and can help late tumours spread. How can one signal give opposite answers, and what holds it back?

scenes.tts: Watch how a Smad complex meets DNA. Its DNA-binding domain reads a tiny four-base tag, such as GTCT, and grips it weakly. Each base is one of four letters, so a four-base tag appears by chance about once every two hundred fifty-six bases. That is millions of times across a human genome. A Smad complex alone cannot pick a gene.
scenes.caption: Watch how a Smad complex meets DNA. Its DNA-binding domain reads a tiny four-base tag, such as GTCT, and grips it weakly. Each base is one of four letters, so a four-base tag appears by chance about once every 256 bases. That is millions of times across a human genome. A Smad complex alone cannot pick a gene.
scenes.visual: Zoom onto a horizontal scrolling DNA ribbon inside the nucleus (schematic). Bright tiny notches marked 'GTCT' flash repeatedly every short stretch along the ribbon; a clean on-screen overlay shows '4 bases: 1 in 256 bp (millions of sites)'. The emerald/violet Smad trimer tries to settle on one notch, wobbles, and slips off. Empathy fix: Show '4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 256' beside the overlay as it is spoken.

scenes.tts: Each cell type makes its own partner transcription factors and keeps its own chromatin open. A Smad complex usually locks onto DNA firmly only beside a partner reading a nearby sequence. The Smad carries one message: TGF beta is here. The partners decide what that means.
scenes.caption: Each cell type makes its own partner transcription factors and keeps its own chromatin open. A Smad complex usually locks onto DNA firmly only beside a partner reading a nearby sequence. The Smad carries one message: TGF-β is here. The partners decide what that means.
scenes.visual: The DNA ribbon splits into two side-by-side panels labelled 'Epithelial nucleus' and 'Fibroblast nucleus', each with an identical emerald/violet Smad trimer hovering over its DNA. In the left epithelial nucleus, a terracotta partner block docks onto an open DNA region right beside 'GTCT', locking the emerald/violet Smad trimer firmly in place. In the right fibroblast nucleus, a differently shaped sky-blue partner block docks beside 'GTCT' on a different open DNA region, anchoring an identical Smad trimer.
scenes.narration: Each cell type makes its own partner transcription factors and keeps its own chromatin open. A Smad complex usually locks onto DNA firmly only beside a partner reading a nearby sequence. The Smad carries one message: TGF-β is here. The partners decide what that means.

scenes.tts: In many epithelial cells, partners turn on p fifteen and p twenty-one to stop division, and shut off Myc. In fibroblasts, different partners switch on collagen genes. Early in cancer, TGF beta restrains tumours because cells obey the stop order. Later, in cells that escape arrest, TGF beta can push them to move, and it quiets nearby immune cells.
scenes.caption: In many epithelial cells, partners turn on p15 and p21 to stop division, and shut off Myc. In fibroblasts, different partners switch on collagen genes. Early in cancer, TGF-β restrains tumours because cells obey the stop order. Later, in cells that escape arrest, TGF-β can push them to move, and it quiets nearby immune cells.
scenes.visual: Left epithelial panel illuminates green upward arrows at 'p15, p21 ↑' and a muted downward arrow at 'Myc ↓' ('Stop dividing'). Right fibroblast panel lights up 'Collagen ↑' ('Matrix / repair'). Then the left panel transitions into 'Late tumour': the p15/p21 arrest bar breaks in two, while a side arrow from the intact Smad complex lights up 'Motility & immune quieting'.

scenes.tts: Pause and predict. Suppose a tissue's matrix holds plenty of TGF beta protein, yet nearby cells show no Smad signal. What could keep that protein away from its receptors?
scenes.caption: Pause and predict. Suppose a tissue's matrix holds plenty of TGF-β protein, yet nearby cells show no Smad signal. What could keep that protein away from its receptors?
scenes.visual: Camera pulls smoothly out of the nucleus back up to the exact membrane cross-section from the first film (amber/cyan/indigo palette preserved). Grey extracellular matrix fibres run above the membrane with many amber TGF-β dimers lying among them (schematic); below, the cyan Type II and indigo Type I receptors stay dark and unphosphorylated. A high-contrast question card enters across the bottom: 'Plenty of TGF-β nearby, receptors silent. What keeps it away?'
scenes.narration: Pause and predict. Suppose a tissue's matrix holds plenty of TGF-β protein, yet nearby cells show no Smad signal. What could keep that protein away from its receptors?

scenes.visual: Question card remains steady at the bottom while a slow progress arc sweeps around its edge. Above, the amber dimers drift very slightly among the grey matrix fibres while the dark receptors wait below, so the frame stays in gentle motion without revealing the answer.

scenes.tts: A signal this powerful must stay off most of the time. Three layered brakes hold it back. First, TGF beta is made with a wrapper piece. The wrapper is cut free but stays clamped around it, tethered to the extracellular matrix. Active dimer is freed locally, for example when an integrin pulls or a protease cuts.
scenes.caption: A signal this powerful must stay off most of the time. Three layered brakes hold it back. First, TGF-β is made with a wrapper piece. The wrapper is cut free but stays clamped around it, tethered to the extracellular matrix. Active dimer is freed locally, for example when an integrin pulls or a protease cuts.
scenes.visual: Question card clears on the carried membrane view. The amber TGF-β dimers among the matrix fibres are now revealed sealed inside slate-grey precursor cages tethered to extracellular matrix fibres ('Brake 1: Latent wrapper'). On one side a membrane integrin grips and tugs the cage open; on the other a small scissor icon ('Protease') snips it, popping one amber dimer free toward cyan Type II. Empathy fix: Label the wrapped dimer 'Cut, but still bound (latent)'.
scenes.narration: A signal this powerful must stay off most of the time. Three layered brakes hold it back. First, TGF-β is made with a wrapper piece. The wrapper is cut free but stays clamped around it, tethered to the extracellular matrix. Active dimer is freed locally, for example when an integrin pulls or a protease cuts.

scenes.tts: Second, the active signal makes its own inhibitor inside the cell. Active Smads switch on the gene for inhibitory Smad seven. Smad seven returns to cap the active type one receptor, blocking incoming Smads in negative feedback. Smad six plays a similar role, preferring the BMP branch.
scenes.caption: Second, the active signal makes its own inhibitor inside the cell. Active Smads switch on the gene for inhibitory Smad7. Smad7 returns to cap the active type I receptor, blocking incoming Smads in negative feedback. Smad6 plays a similar role, preferring the BMP branch.
scenes.visual: Carried membrane-to-nucleus cross-section. From the glowing nuclear edge, crimson blocks labelled 'Smad7' emerge and rise up to the active indigo Type I receptor ('Brake 2: Smad7 feedback'). Crimson Smad7 snaps onto Type I's docking site, physically bouncing an approaching emerald R-Smad away.
scenes.narration: Second, the active signal makes its own inhibitor inside the cell. Active Smads switch on the gene for inhibitory Smad7. Smad7 returns to cap the active type I receptor, blocking incoming Smads in negative feedback. Smad6 plays a similar role, preferring the BMP branch.

scenes.tts: Third, Smad seven recruits ubiquitin ligases called Smurfs to the active receptor. Smurfs tag the receptor, and some Smads, with ubiquitin for destruction. Together, these layered brakes keep signaling local and brief. Breaking a key part, like Smad four or the GS safety catch, can drive human disease.
scenes.caption: Third, Smad7 recruits ubiquitin ligases called Smurfs to the active receptor. Smurfs tag the receptor, and some Smads, with ubiquitin for destruction. Together, these layered brakes keep signaling local and brief. Breaking a key part, like Smad4 or the GS safety catch, can drive human disease.
scenes.visual: Carried membrane view. Crimson Smad7 on indigo Type I pulls in a burnt-amber block ('Smurf ligase', 'Brake 3: Ubiquitin destruction'). Small gold ubiquitin beads chain onto the indigo receptor, which pulls downward into a fading degradation ring while the pathway dims back to quiet rest.
scenes.narration: Third, Smad7 recruits ubiquitin ligases called Smurfs to the active receptor. Smurfs tag the receptor, and some Smads, with ubiquitin for destruction. Together, these layered brakes keep signaling local and brief. Breaking a key part, like Smad4 or the GS safety catch, can drive human disease.

scenes.tts: So one short relay depends on both context and control. Inside the nucleus, partner factors and open chromatin decide which genes respond to TGF beta. Outside and at the membrane, layered brakes decide where and how long the signal lasts.
scenes.caption: So one short relay depends on both context and control. Inside the nucleus, partner factors and open chromatin decide which genes respond to TGF-β. Outside and at the membrane, layered brakes decide where and how long the signal lasts.
scenes.visual: Full cross-section settles into clean balance: above the membrane, the slate latent cage holds amber TGF-β in check; at the membrane, crimson Smad7 and burnt-amber Smurf fade the receptor glow; below in the nucleus, terracotta and sky-blue partners beside emerald/violet Smad complexes glow cleanly on DNA.
scenes.narration: So one short relay depends on both context and control. Inside the nucleus, partner factors and open chromatin decide which genes respond to TGF-β. Outside and at the membrane, layered brakes decide where and how long the signal lasts.

scenes.visual: Clean dark navy end card with a subtle horizontal emerald-to-crimson rule above a single centred line in crisp white type, nothing underneath: 'Partner factors choose Smad targets, and layered brakes restrain the signal.'
